poll_interruption.cause: The session container restarted mid-poll and killed four in-flight managers: Opus 5 mean reversion, Opus Value, Sonnet contrarian turnarounds, Sonnet deep value.
poll_interruption.handling: All four were re-polled with the identical packet and the same 2026-09-04 price cutoff, so every manager in the field decided on the same information. No book filled on a default in the interim — the interruption happened before anything was written to weeks/.

desk_errors_recorded: The re-poll prompt for Opus Value repeated a stale fact from the desk's own notes — that its Round 2 book held BTC spot alongside a 2x BTC perp. That was true of an earlier leg, not the live one. The manager checked its packet, said so plainly, and traded the packet. The desk was wrong and the manager was right; the outcome was unaffected, but a desk that feeds a manager a false position is a real failure mode and it is recorded rather than quietly dropped.

One manager reported that another agent overwrote a working file it had left in the shared scratchpad. Every decision file was checked against the register afterwards and none was cross-contaminated; five files carried the file stem in their name field instead of the display name, which the writer normalises. Managers were told from that point to keep working files in their own directories.
research_access: Every manager had WebSearch and WebFetch. The session-wide WebSearch quota (200 calls) was exhausted partway through the poll, and four managers — Opus-fleet deep value, Opus 5 pairs, Opus-fleet price momentum, Opus-fleet small/mid-cap growth — reported working from WebFetch plus their own Yahoo price pulls instead. This is an unequal-information artefact of the desk's plumbing, not of the managers, and it is recorded here because it is not visible anywhere else.
reasoning_invariant: Every decision carries a stated reason; enforced by tracker/check_reasoning.py.

decisions.reason: Week 8 (leg 3): a targeted resize, not a rebuild. The AI-infra fundamentals did not change - NVDA guided Q3 to $108B, ANET printed its first $3B quarter, TSMC sales +45%, MU is at ~6x forward with $100B contracted revenue into its Sept 30 print - so the core stays. Two legs did change character: (1) GEV is the one name where the story deteriorated on its own - it slid to ~$887 on Aug 31 while VRT and ETN were flat and GRID was up, i.e. single-name repricing on the ~$400M 2026 Wind EBITDA loss guide plus a CFO handoff, and it carries the most premium multiple in the book into a rate shock; I cut it from 10% to 4% rather than to zero because the $176B backlog and 88% order growth are real. BTC weight is untouched (35bps/side churn is not worth paying for a leg that is doing its job at +20%). No stops on the conviction core, consistent with the strategy of record: this book already survived a -14.6% drawdown intact and a 15% stop would have converted that into a realized loss.

Week 8 (leg 2): the rate cycle this book was built to rotate with has turned, so the book rotates. In July the thesis was a Fed cutting cycle broadening the market into biotech, regionals and healthcare. This week: 10-year at 4.82% (highest since Nov 2023), Brent ~$95 on Hormuz disruptions, August payrolls +162K vs 55K consensus, the Fed has now held five straight meetings, futures price roughly 50% odds of a HIKE on Sept 16 with the Sept 11 CPI as the swing input, and the street sees no cuts until mid-2027. Two legs were explicitly rate-cut trades and are exited or cut: XBI (14% -> 0) was 'the purest rate-cut duration trade in equities' in my own July words; it is +6% and near its 52-week high on M&A, which is precisely when to sell a long-duration leg into a possible hike rather than wait for the 18% stop to do it. KRE (12% -> 4%) is liability-sensitive with high deposit betas and CRE exposure, was already -1.9% and lagging XLF; hike odds are the single worst input for it. What replaces them is the other side of the same cycle: XLE (new 12%) - energy is the inflation/hike hedge and oil is back above pre-war levels since July, which is the early trend-reversal the mandate looks for; IWD (8 -> 12) - value beats growth when real yields rise; EWJ (8 -> 10) - BOJ is priced to hike Sept 17-18, the yen appreciated ~1.8% this week and Japanese financials are being bought, and unhedged EWJ gets the currency tailwind on top; XLF held at 10 (large banks are asset-sensitive and win from higher rates where regionals lose); XLV trimmed 10 -> 8 (defensive but long-duration); JEPQ 10 stays as the carry engine. ETH 5 / SOL 3 stay at identical weights (crypto churn is 35bps/side and the trend is intact - BTC's largest ETF inflow in nine months this week), with stops re-anchored to the new fill. Cash goes 20% -> 26%: at 4% APY it is a genuine carry position and the right size to be holding into a CPI-then-FOMC week where the coin can land either way. Every equity leg keeps a stop as the mandate requires. Novelty vs my Round 2 book: zero symbol overlap (R2 is MU/AMD/NVDA/GEV/TSM/VRT/ANET/BTC) - no AI-capex thesis anywhere here.

The barbell was rebuilt on 8/31 specifically for a Warsh Fed that welcomes higher yields, and this week's tape confirmed that regime rather than changing it: August payrolls printed +162k vs ~53k consensus, the 2yr moved to ~4.37-4.40% and the 10yr to ~4.78-4.80%, and CME odds of a hike at the Sept 15-16 FOMC rose from 49% to 58%. The book absorbed that shock as designed -- NAV +4.10% vs SPY +2.59%, max drawdown under 2% -- because 30% of it earns 4% in cash and 35% sits in BRK-B/KO/MRK/JNJ/XLU that a hawkish-again Fed favors (utilities were the only green sector Friday). The aggressive sleeve's fundamentals got stronger, not weaker: NVDA closed the $12.9B Hugging Face deal and trades ~$230, 2% from its high, on a $96.2B quarter; AVGO's dip to ~$358 after beating its own $16B AI-revenue target by $700M and guiding FY27 AI revenue to double to $115B is a price/fundamentals disconnect I want to own, not sell, and the -20% stop already bounds it; GEV won the Venezuela grid-modernization mandate. The one leg the hawkish print genuinely hurts is GLD (gold -1.4% to ~$4,477 on real yields and the dollar), but it was already trimmed to 4% last week for exactly this reason and is too small to churn. Holding beats trading because (a) the legs are four sessions old and a replacement would pay ~3bps of round-trip friction plus reset every stop reference for no change in thesis, (b) the next two weeks are binary macro -- PPI 9/10, CPI 9/11, FOMC 9/16 -- and reshaping a hedged book into those events on the strength of one Friday jobs number is noise-chasing, and (c) the mandate's contrarian BTC perp stays off: BTC printed a four-month high of $82.2k and then fell to ~$79.3k on the hike repricing, which is neither the flush that earns a contrarian entry nor a level worth paying 10% APR funding to chase. No leg is near a stop; nothing has changed that the book was not already built to handle.

The weekly re-rank makes one swap and one resize; everything else holds on evidence. SWAP: GDX (6%) exits and XLE (8%) enters. Both are commodity-beta sectors but the Sept 4 jobs print (+162k vs ~53k, hike odds 49%->58%, 2yr ~4.40%, 10yr ~4.80%, dollar up) pushes them in opposite directions: gold fell ~1.4-2% to ~$4,380-4,480 as real yields and the dollar rose, and gold miners were among the day's worst groups -- the second violent reversal in two weeks for a leg I had already cut and tightened after Warsh's Jackson Hole speech, so the momentum-exhaustion read is now confirmed rather than suspected. XLE meanwhile was August's top Select Sector fund (+7.4%), made a 52-week high on Monday's US-Iran strikes and the Hormuz tanker attack, sits at $64.06 vs a $65.52 high with WTI ~$91 and Brent ~$96, and is the sector the sell-side names as an outperformer if the Fed hikes -- the same macro shock that hurts gold helps energy, so the swap raises the book's alignment with the regime without adding a new factor. It also keeps the correlation dedupe honest: one commodity-beta long, not two. RESIZE: XHB short 5%->6%. The thesis strengthened this week -- 10yr at 4.8% (from 4.1% at the start of the year), 30-year mortgage 6.7%, new home sales at the lowest level since January, XHB -8.5% over one year and 16% below its 52-week high -- and Friday's +1% bounce is a better short entry inside an intact downtrend. KRE at 10% (+2.3% on the leg, higher highs since the June breakout) benefits from a Fed that keeps the front end high while the 2s/10s curve stays positive ~+40-50bp. XLI at 9% was the best sector on Friday and stays the least consumer-levered cyclical. XLV at 8% keeps the health-care rotation; its Friday weakness is a one-day give-back inside a leadership trend. XLY short at 7% was strengthened by Lululemon's -18% guidance cut and discretionary being the weakest sector on the day. MSOS short stays at 4% -- the June DEA hearing catalyst I flagged has passed, the ETF is still ~30% below its June high, and the -12% stop covers the Friday +3% squeeze; at 12bps per side under $15 it is not worth churning. NET: gross rises 61%->64%, longs 45->47, shorts 16->17, cash 39->36 still earning 4% into PPI 9/10, CPI 9/11 and the FOMC 9/16. Round 3 novelty: zero ticker overlap with my Round 2 book (NVDA/AVGO/GEV/ANET/BRK-B/KO/MRK/JNJ/XLU/GLD), so same-direction gross-weight overlap is 0%.

The regime under this book changed materially in the last five sessions and two of my legs were positioned for the opposite of it. Warsh's Jackson Hole speech on 8/31 pushed September hike odds from ~35% to ~60-67%, and Friday's August payrolls print (162k vs 55k expected, unemployment 4.1%) confirmed it: 2y yields rose 4bp to 4.37%, the S&P fell 0.38% and the dollar has resurged hard enough to erase EM currencies' entire 2026 gain. EMLC is EM local-currency debt - a hawkish Fed and a bid dollar is the single worst input for it, and it was my best performer (+0.59%) so I am selling strength rather than a loss. NLY's entire sell-side case rests on 'two 25bp cuts later in 2026' cutting repo funding costs; with the market now pricing a hike into the 3.50-3.75% range on 9/16, that thesis is inverted, and higher rate volatility is what damages agency-MBS book value regardless of the 13% dividend. This book (-2.50% NAV, badly lagging SPY +3.62% and BTC +23.17% over the same stretch) has been sitting in four unconfirmed, half-committed positions -- KRE, XLV, XBI, USMV -- with no short leg despite a mandate that explicitly calls for gold-miner/semi mean reversion and a defensive-vs-discretionary pair. decisions.name: Sonnet global diversification via US-listed ADRs and ETFs

The dominant event this week was the August jobs report: nonfarm payrolls printed +162k vs a ~55k forecast (prior month revised to just 21k) with unemployment steady at 4.1%. This week's news mostly confirmed rather than challenged the book's core rotation thesis, so I made targeted size changes instead of a rebuild. Healthcare/biotech: reporting this week put 2026 biotech M&A on track for its best year since pre-COVID (~$106B in deals through mid-year), described healthcare as a 'haven for investors ditching tech,' and flagged XBI approaching a breakout toward its 2021 high near $174.79 off a bullish flag -- strong enough to add to the winning leg (11% -> 14%), funded by a small trim to XLV (17% -> 16%) which is working but has less specific fresh catalyst news this week. Regional banks: coverage this week ('Small Banks Are Finally Gaining on Their Giant Rivals,' 'Main Street Banks Are a Cheaper Way to Play the AI Banking Boom') plus ongoing deregulation and excess-capital tailwinds support adding to KRE (12% -> 14%); XLF held flat at 13% as the broader financials beneficiary. SMH is near 52-week highs (98.6% 1-year total return) and the leg is already down -3.7% against us; JPMorgan is recommending buying the semis dip and Nvidia was up on the day, which directly fights the short. This book was too conservative to be a momentum book: 46% cash and no shorts left NAV at -5.78% while SPY ran +2.59%. Meanwhile the tape this week showed exactly the kind of clean, tradeable momentum this mandate is built for: XLE was the best-performing SPDR sector in August (+7.4%) and is still +49% YTD on Middle East supply risk; SMH is near its 52-week high with a +2.6% day and +98.6% 1yr return on AI-infrastructure demand; XBI is in a bullish-flag breakout approaching its 2021 high on M&A momentum. On the other side, Friday's stronger-than-expected August payrolls report (+162k, the biggest August beat in ~30 years) revived rate-hike odds and pushed Treasury yields to a 19-month high, breaking TLT's price trend and pressuring rate-sensitive regional banks (KRE, already -2.74% in this book's live P&L). I'm cutting cash from 46% to 15%, dropping the underweight XLF/XLV sector bets that were merely riding the tape rather than leading it, concentrating new capital in the actual momentum leaders (XLE, SMH, XBI), keeping a smaller IWM stake for small-cap breadth, and adding two shorts (TLT, KRE) so the book expresses genuine long-strength/short-weakness momentum instead of sitting on the sidelines.

Nothing that happened this week breaks the thesis on any name in the book, and the drawdown legs are macro noise, not fundamental deterioration. AVGO (-15.27%, worst leg) actually reported a beat-and-raise this week -- tripled AI chip sales and CEO Hock Tan guiding AI revenue growth out through 2028 -- yet the stock sold off ('Someone Must Know Something' headlines, 'Is It Too Soon to Buy the Dip?'), which reads as valuation digestion after a big run, not a broken moat. LLY (-6.57%) announced a major acquisition and drew bullish sell-side commentary ('Great News for Eli Lilly Stock Investors') the same week it fell -- again a macro-driven pullback, not a company-specific problem. The common thread across all three: the August jobs report (released Sept 4-5) came in stronger than expected, and Fed funds futures for the Sept 16 FOMC flipped from favoring a cut to now pricing better-than-even odds of a HIKE (roughly 58% for 3.75-4.00% vs 42% for holding at 3.50-3.75%, versus roughly 50/50 the day before). That is a genuine regime-risk data point, but it hits high-multiple/duration assets broadly and is exactly why this book already carries a cash buffer and a tactical IWM short rather than being run at full gross. If anything, the jobs-driven rate-hike repricing argues for keeping the short: small caps carry more leverage and refinancing risk than the balance-sheet-strength compounders in this book, and GuruFocus flagged IWM as ~52% overvalued on GF Value this week, reinforcing that leg. V and MA are working (+4.00% / +2.85%), payments volumes remain resilient, and UNH/COST are in normal-range drawdowns with no adverse company news found. Replacing the book now would mean selling AVGO/GOOGL/LLY into exactly the kind of macro overreaction a quality-compounder mandate is supposed to look through, while paying real transaction costs to do it. Holding costs nothing and keeps the existing cash-plus-hedge structure intact into the Sept 16 FOMC, which is the actual event that will resolve this week's rate-path uncertainty.

This book's core premise -- imminent Fed rate cuts driving a carry trade in regional banks, financials and small caps -- was directly contradicted by this week's data. The August jobs report (released Sept 4-5) beat estimates hard enough that Fed funds futures for the Sept 16 FOMC swung from a plurality favoring a cut to now pricing better-than-even odds (~58%) of a HIKE to 3.75-4.00%, an 8-point swing in a single day.
